title: Apply elementary farm layout and infrastructure

lessons.title: Knowing the farm layout
lessons.html:
What is farm layout?

Farm layout is the way the farm is set out: where the fields, camps, buildings, roads and water points are. A good layout saves time, money and effort. It also keeps people, animals and crops safe.

Parts of a farm

  • Fields or lands: where crops grow.
  • Camps: fenced areas of veld or pasture for animals.
  • Kraal: a strong pen near the yard for holding animals at night or for handling.
  • Handling facilities: crush pen, loading ramp, dip tank.
  • Buildings: sheds, stores, workshop, packhouse, offices and houses.
  • Water points: boreholes, dams, tanks, troughs.
  • Roads and tracks: for the bakkie, tractor and trucks.
  • Gates: to move between camps and fields.

Reading a simple farm map

Many farms have a map on the office wall. Each camp or field has a name or number, for example Camp 4 or Land B. Learn the names. When your supervisor says, "Move the heifers to Camp 6," you must know where that is and which gates to use.

Why things are placed where they are

  • The chemical store is far from houses, the kitchen and water, to keep people safe.
  • The kraal is near the yard so animals can be watched.
  • Crop fields are near water for irrigation.
  • Roads follow high ground so they do not flood.
  • Camps share water points so one trough can serve two camps.

When you understand the layout, you can do your job faster and avoid mistakes, such as leaving cattle in a camp with no water or driving a tractor through a planted land.

lessons.title: Looking after farm infrastructure
lessons.html:
What is infrastructure?

Infrastructure is the fixed things the farm needs to work: fences, gates, roads, pipes, troughs, buildings, power lines and handling facilities. It costs a lot of money to build, so we must look after it.

Fences and gates

  • Walk or drive the fence lines as instructed. Look for broken wire, loose droppers and fallen posts.
  • Always leave a gate as you found it, unless told otherwise. An open gate can let cattle into a maize land or onto the road.
  • Report holes under fences where animals or jackals get through.

Water infrastructure

  • Check troughs, pipes and ball valves for leaks.
  • Check that the windmill or pump is working and the tank is filling.
  • Report problems quickly. Animals can die without water in hot weather.

Roads and tracks

  • Drive only on farm roads, not through fields or camps.
  • Report washed-out roads and blocked drains.

Buildings and handling facilities

  • Keep sheds and stores clean and tidy.
  • Report broken rails in the crush pen or kraal. Broken rails can hurt animals and people.
  • Keep doors to the chemical store and fuel store locked.

Safety

Wear gloves when working with fencing wire, because it can cut deeply. Watch for wire that springs back when cut. Never climb on a windmill or tank without permission and safety equipment. Stay away from electric fences and power lines unless you are trained.

Reporting

Tell your supervisor what you found, where it is, and how bad it is. For example: "Camp 3, north fence, two posts down near the dam." Clear reports help the farm fix things quickly.

Key points

  • Learn the names and places of camps, fields and buildings.
  • Leave gates as you found them.
  • Check fences, troughs and pipes and report damage clearly.
  • Keep chemical and fuel stores locked and away from water and houses.
  • Wear gloves and work safely with wire and machines.
